problems.stem: You want to show how monthly sales changed across Jan, Feb, Mar, and Apr. Which chart type best answers a 'how did it change over time' question?
options: A pie chart with one slice per month.
A line chart with months on the horizontal axis and sales on the vertical axis.
A doughnut chart of the four months.
A 3-D exploded pie chart for visual interest.
problems.explanation: A line chart maps a value against an ordered axis like time, so the rise and fall across months is easy to read. Pie charts show parts of a whole at one moment, not change over time.

problems.stem: A column chart of donations runs from 2018 to 2024. The vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0, so a rise from 95 to 100 looks like the bars doubled. What is the honest fix?
options: Keep the axis at 90 because it fills the chart nicely.
Start the value axis at 0 so the bar heights are proportional to the actual numbers.
Add more gridlines so the change looks smaller.
Switch to a darker color so the bars stand out.
problems.explanation: A truncated axis exaggerates small differences. For bar and column charts, starting the value axis at 0 keeps the heights proportional to the data so the reader is not misled.

problems.stem: Your chart is titled 'Sales Chart'. The point you actually found is that the West region outsold every other region. Which title best helps the reader?
options: 'Sales Chart' because it names what the chart is.
'West Region Led Q1 Sales by a Wide Margin' because it states the finding the reader should take away.
'Data Visualization' because it describes the genre.
problems.explanation: A claim-first title tells the reader the finding, not just the topic. The chart then becomes the evidence for that one stated point.

problems.stem: You need to compare total revenue across five separate stores for one quarter. Which chart answers that comparison most clearly?
options: A line chart connecting the five stores.
A bar (or column) chart with one bar per store so heights compare directly.
A pie chart that hides the exact totals.
A scatter plot of store number against revenue.
problems.explanation: A bar chart compares discrete categories like separate stores by bar height. A line chart implies a connected sequence, which the five unrelated stores do not form.
